html:
A magnetised needle that swings to point north and south, used to find direction. In Song China, Shen Kuo gave the first clear description of it in his Dream Pool Essays of 1088, and by about 1100 Chinese ships were steering by it.

The idea is older. Under the Han dynasty, the Chinese used a spoon of lodestone, a naturally magnetic rock, on a bronze plate for divination and for siting buildings by feng shui. Song craftsmen learned to magnetise iron needles by rubbing them on lodestone, and to float or hang them so they could turn freely. Shen Kuo also noticed that the needle does not point exactly to true north, the first known record of magnetic declination.

Sailors took it up because it worked when clouds hid the sun and stars. It helped Song and later Ming ships cross the seas to Southeast Asia and the Indian Ocean.

How it spread:

  • The first record in Western Europe is from around 1190, and in the Islamic world in the 13th century. Whether they learned it from China or found it on their own is still debated.
  • Europeans added the dry pivot and the compass card.

It is one of the Four Great Inventions of China, with paper, printing and gunpowder. Without it, the long ocean voyages of Zheng He and later of the Portuguese and Spanish would have been far harder.
